HuYgTa-159627-d1e114.summary: Title paragraph restating the question in verse-like rubric form: whether any sin is simply irremissible.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e123.summary: States the formal question to be disputed: whether some sin is simply irremissible.
claims: The question to be resolved is whether any sin is simply irremissible.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e130.summary: Argument for the affirmative: one should pray for the remission of every remissible sin, but there is a sin for which one is not to pray for remission, per 1 John: 'there is a sin unto death, for which I do not say that one should pray'; therefore there is a sin that is simply irremissible.
claims: Since Scripture (1 John) forbids praying for remission of the 'sin unto death,' that sin must be simply irremissible.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e147.summary: Argument for the negative: no evil whose root or power derives from God is simply irremissible; but the power to sin, of whatever kind of sin, is from God (as will be shown below); therefore no sin is simply irremissible. Sets out the plan of the question in four parts, corresponding to distinctions 43 and 44: (1) whether there is a sin against the Holy Spirit, (2) whether such sin is irremissible, (3) whether every power to sin is from God, (4) whether every power to dominate/rule is from God.
claims: Since the power to sin derives from God, no sin can be simply irremissible in an unqualified sense.

The question divides into four parts across distinctions 43-44: the existence of sin against the Holy Spirit, its irremissibility, the divine origin of the power to sin, and the divine origin of the power to dominate.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e173.summary: States the author's resolutio in advance: although no sin, considered in relation to divine power, can be called irremissible, yet from divine and inspired Scripture we know there is a certain sin against the Holy Spirit which is rightly called irremissible, not because it lacks the power to be remitted absolutely (since even its power to sin flowed from God), but because it contains within itself no attached circumstance excusing the sin.
claims: No sin is irremissible with respect to God's absolute power.
Sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible because it contains no excusing circumstance, not because God lacks power to remit it.
concepts: irremissibility as lack of excusing circumstance vs. lack of divine power

HuYgTa-159627-d1e195.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 1, restating its question: whether there is a sin against the Holy Spirit.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e206.summary: Answers Article 1 affirmatively: it is plain from Sacred Scripture (the Gospel) that there is a sin called sin against the Holy Spirit. Given this, announces two further matters to be examined: first, what sin against the Holy Spirit is; second, how many such sins there are.
claims: Scripture plainly attests the existence of sin against the Holy Spirit.
concepts: scriptural basis for sin against the Holy Spirit

HuYgTa-159627-d1e224.summary: Explains what sin against the Holy Spirit is by first distinguishing two senses of 'Holy Spirit': essentially (applying to the whole Trinity, as in John 4, 'God is spirit...') and personally (the third person alone). Scripture takes the essential sense when it speaks of sin against the Holy Spirit, distinguishing it from blasphemy against Christ's humanity (which is remissible) versus against his deity (irremissible), illustrated by the Jews' blasphemies against Christ (calling him a glutton and friend of sinners, then attributing his exorcisms to Beelzebub), to which Christ responds (Matthew 12) that whoever speaks against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor the next. Notes that the ancient doctors (Athanasius, Hilary, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome) understood sin against the Holy Spirit this way, whereas modern doctors instead apply the term to sinning against what is personally appropriated to the Holy Spirit (divine will, goodness, clemency).
claims: 'Holy Spirit' in Scripture's talk of this sin is taken essentially (as deity), not merely personally (as the third person).
Blasphemy against Christ's humanity is remissible, but blasphemy against his deity (identified with sinning against the Holy Spirit) is irremissible, per Matthew 12:32.
Ancient doctors understood sin against the Holy Spirit essentially; modern doctors understand it as sinning against qualities personally appropriated to the Holy Spirit.
concepts: essential vs. personal predication in Trinitarian theology
blasphemy against Christ's humanity vs. deity

HuYgTa-159627-d1e297.summary: Surveys differing opinions on the number and distinction of sins against the Holy Spirit: some hold there are four (despair, presumption, impugning known truth — especially truth of faith, and envy/rivalry toward a neighbor's grace); others add obstinacy and the resolve never to repent, making six; still others add sin from deliberate malice (called sin from choice or sin from habit) and final impenitence, making eight.
claims: One tradition counts four sins against the Holy Spirit: despair, presumption, impugning known truth, and envy of others' grace.
A second tradition adds obstinacy and resolve never to repent, for six.
A third tradition adds sin from deliberate malice/habit and final impenitence, for eight.
concepts: taxonomies of sin against the Holy Spirit

HuYgTa-159627-d1e331.summary: Proposes a fourfold analytic framework to organize the distinction among these sins: they can be considered in relation to the physician, the medicine, the sick person, and the sickness.
claims: The various proposed sins against the Holy Spirit can be organized by reference to physician, medicine, patient, and sickness.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e344.summary: Applies the 'physician' category: despair and presumption are taken with respect to the physician (God), since despairers attend only to God's justice, ignoring his mercy (illustrated by Cain's 'my iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon' and Bernard's saying about the ingratitude that dries up the fountain of mercy), while the presumptuous attend only to God's mercy, fearing nothing of his justice.
claims: Despair arises from attending only to divine justice while ignoring divine mercy (as with Cain).
Presumption arises from attending only to divine mercy while fearing nothing of divine justice.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e381.summary: Applies the 'medicine' category (faith and grace): impugning the truth of the faith and envying grace conferred on one's brothers both render the medicine of faith and grace useless to the sinner.
claims: Impugning the truth of faith and envying a neighbor's grace are considered with respect to the 'medicine' (faith and grace), which such sins render ineffective for the sinner.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e397.summary: Applies the 'patient' and 'sickness' categories: on the side of the patient (the sinner), obstinacy is a pertinacious conversion to a mutable good, while impenitence is a pertinacious turning away from the immutable good without the resolve to return to it; on the side of the sickness itself, sin from choice/deliberate malice is a vicious habit (the mind's basest infirmity), and final impenitence is the culminating, death-bound disease of any mortal sin.
claims: Obstinacy and impenitence are distinguished by reference to the sinner (patient): pertinacious attachment to a mutable good versus pertinacious rejection of the immutable good.
Sin from deliberate malice and final impenitence are distinguished by reference to the sickness itself: a vicious habit versus the terminal disease of mortal sin.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e428.summary: Draws the article's conclusion: the first four (despair, presumption, impugning the faith, envy of grace) are more properly called sins, being distinct and determinate species of sin with distinct subject matter, whereas the remaining four (obstinacy, impenitence-as-resolve, habitual malice, final impenitence) are better called circumstances or consequences of sin, since they lack a determinate matter and can attach to any kind of mortal sin. The author therefore approves the position of those doctors who hold there are four kinds of sin against the Holy Spirit.
claims: The first four items are properly distinct species of sin; the latter four are better classified as circumstances or sequelae applicable to any mortal sin.
The author endorses the position that there are properly four kinds of sin against the Holy Spirit.
concepts: species of sin vs. circumstantiae/sequelae of sin
final adjudication of the fourfold count

HuYgTa-159627-d1e461.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 2, restating its question: whether sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible.
concepts: irremissibility of sin against the Holy Spirit

HuYgTa-159627-d1e473.summary: States the article's main conclusion: with respect to divine power, no sin is irremissible.
claims: No sin is irremissible relative to divine power itself.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e482.summary: Proof/first point: God could, if he willed, remit the sins of the living and the dead, demons and humans alike; but calling a sin 'remissible' in the sense of retaining an aptitude or fittingness for remission, every sin against the Holy Spirit can in that sense be called irremissible — for whereas sin from ignorance, passion, or impotence is somewhat excused and thereby retains an aptitude for remission, sin against the Holy Spirit has no attached excusing circumstance, only an aggravating one, and so carries no such aptitude toward its own remission.
claims: God's absolute power could remit any sin whatsoever.

Sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible in the qualified sense that, unlike excusable sins, it lacks any circumstance conferring an aptitude for remission — it has only aggravating, never excusing, circumstances.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e517.summary: Second argument, by analogy with bodily sickness: bodily infirmity is called incurable when it disposes the sick person to abominate all food and abhor and refuse all medicine, per Psalm 106 ('their soul abhorred all food, and they drew near to the gates of death'); similarly one who sins against the Holy Spirit abhors spiritual medicine, as shown previously.
claims: By analogy with an incurable bodily sickness that makes the patient reject all food and medicine, one who sins against the Holy Spirit likewise abhors spiritual medicine, supporting the sin's 'irremissible' character.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e535.summary: Third argument: no mortal sin is remitted without penitence; but every sin against the Holy Spirit somehow makes the sinner impenitent; therefore any such sin can be called irremissible.
claims: Since remission of mortal sin requires penitence, and sin against the Holy Spirit induces impenitence, such sin can be called irremissible in that qualified sense.
concepts: impenitence induced by sin against the Holy Spirit

HuYgTa-159627-d1e548.summary: Reports a rival position (attributed to certain doctors, tracing to Augustine's understanding of sin against the Holy Spirit as mortal sin joined with final impenitence): on this view such sin is called simply irremissible, since it can never be remitted, neither in this life (final impenitence blocking it) nor in the next (which is not a state of remission).
claims: A rival view (Augustinian in inspiration) holds that sin against the Holy Spirit, understood as mortal sin plus final impenitence, is simply irremissible because remission is impossible both in this life and the next.
concepts: Augustine's definition of sin against the Holy Spirit

HuYgTa-159627-d1e566.summary: First objection against this rival position: it does not seem true, since God's infinite power is not exhausted by the magnitude of any sin whatsoever; therefore God can remit every sin.
claims: God's infinite power cannot be exhausted by any sin's magnitude, so in principle every sin is remissible, against the rival 'simply irremissible' view.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e576.summary: Second objection, citing the commonly reported legend of Trajan: it is widely said that at Gregory's prayers Trajan was freed from hell and resuscitated from the dead to do penance; yet it is plain that Trajan died in many mortal sins (from the massacre of martyrs) and with final impenitence — for had he repented before dying, he would not have been damned for his sins nor resuscitated in order to do penance.
claims: The traditional legend of Trajan's posthumous deliverance through Gregory's prayers is offered as a counterexample: Trajan died in mortal sin with final impenitence, yet was later granted remission — contradicting the claim that such a state is simply irremissible.
concepts: legend of Trajan and Gregory the Great

HuYgTa-159627-d1e596.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 3, restating its question: whether every power to sin is from God.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e609.summary: States the article's main conclusion: the power to sin is from God.
claims: The power to sin derives from God.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e616.summary: First proof (argument 1): every being is from God; the power to sin is some being; therefore it is from God. The major is proved from faith ('without him nothing was made,' John 1:3); the minor is proved because what is purely nothing has no power at all.
claims: Since the power to sin is a genuine being (not pure nothing), and every being is from God (per John 1:3), the power to sin is from God.
concepts: potentia peccandi as a positive being

HuYgTa-159627-d1e627.summary: Second proof (argument 2): the power to do good (benefacere) is from God; therefore so is the power to sin, since the same power underlies both meriting and demeriting — proved because we can do good and merit by rational power, but rational powers extend to opposites, so we can also do evil and demerit by the same power, which is properly what sinning is.
claims: The power to sin is the same power as the power to do good and merit, since rational powers by their nature extend to opposite acts.
concepts: rational powers as powers for opposites (potentiae ad opposita)
identity of meriting and demeriting power

HuYgTa-159627-d1e647.summary: Third proof (argument 3): only the will is properly the power to sin, per Augustine's De libero arbitrio II; but the will is from God; therefore the power to sin is from God.
claims: Since the will (the proper seat of the power to sin, per Augustine) is from God, the power to sin is from God.
concepts: will as proper subject of potentia peccandi

HuYgTa-159627-d1e662.summary: Fourth proof (argument 4): every good is from God; but powers for evil things are themselves good (per Topics III); therefore the power to sin is from God.
claims: Powers for evil acts are themselves classified as good (per Aristotle's Topics), and since every good is from God, the power to sin is from God.
concepts: Aristotle, Topics III on powers for contraries as good

HuYgTa-159627-d1e671.summary: Reports a rival solution via distinction: some doctors say the power to sin can be considered in two ways — as the principle of an act (in which sense it is from God, since whatever has the nature of a positive being must be traced to God as first cause), or as capable of defect/failure (in which sense it is not from God, since defectibility belongs to a created thing from the fact that it is made from nothing — for what, left to itself, tends toward nothing cannot derive that tendency from another, i.e., from God).
claims: A distinguishing solution: the power to sin as a positive principle of act is from God, but its defectibility (capacity to fail) is not from God, since defectibility stems from the creature's origin ex nihilo, which cannot be attributed to God.
concepts: principle of act vs. capacity for defect
defectibility as a consequence of creation ex nihilo

HuYgTa-159627-d1e700.summary: Supporting gloss on the rival distinction: what belongs to something from itself cannot belong to it from another.
claims: A principle underlying the rival distinction: self-derived features cannot simultaneously be externally caused.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e709.summary: Reports a further argument for the same conclusion (that the power to sin is not from God) by other doctors: if the power to sin were from God, this would chiefly be because such power just is free will itself; but this is false, since Anselm (De libero arbitrio) says that sinning is neither liberty nor part of liberty.
claims: A further argument denying that the power to sin (as such) is identical with free will, appealing to Anselm's denial that sinning constitutes or is part of liberty.
concepts: distinguishing free will from the power to sin

HuYgTa-159627-d1e731.summary: Another argument for the negative view: if the power to sin were from God, then sin itself would be from God; but the consequent is false; the inference is proved because act is more perfect than potency, and God's works are perfect (per Deuteronomy), so if the potency (to sin) were from God, the more perfect act (sinning) would be too, absurdly.
claims: If the (defective) power to sin were from God, then by the greater perfection of act over potency and the perfection of God's works, the sinful act itself would have to be from God — an unacceptable consequence.
concepts: Deuteronomy on the perfection of God's works

HuYgTa-159627-d1e742.summary: Final argument for the negative view: whatever has an evil use is itself evil (per Topics III), and consequently cannot be from God; but the use of the power to sin is evil, since that use just is sinning itself; therefore the power to sin cannot be from God.
claims: Since using the power to sin just is sinning (an evil use), and whatever has an evil use is itself evil (per Aristotle), the power to sin cannot be from God.
concepts: Aristotle, Topics III on evil use implying evil nature

HuYgTa-159627-d1e756.summary: The author's assessment of the rival distinction: he judges the conclusion drawn from the first part of the distinction (that the power to sin as principle of act is from God) to be true, but judges the conclusion drawn from the second part (that its defectibility is not from God) to be untenable, since it seems to conflict with the conclusion he himself has posited.
claims: The author accepts that the power to sin qua positive act-principle is from God, but rejects the claim that its defectibility is not from God.
concepts: partial acceptance/rejection of the rival distinction

HuYgTa-159627-d1e769.summary: First argument against the rejected part of the rival distinction: a defect lacking the character of evil is no less from God than a defect that has the character of evil; but a defect with the character of evil (e.g., a penal defect) is from God; the possibility of failing (possibilitas deficiendi), however, does not have the character of moral evil, since every evil is either the evil of fault (culpa) or of punishment (poena), and the possibility of failing has neither, since it existed in the state of innocence, prior to all fault and punishment.
claims: The mere possibility of failing (defectibility) does not have the character of moral evil (fault or punishment), since it predates the Fall, and hence — like penal defects, which are admittedly from God — should also be traced to God.
concepts: evil of fault vs. evil of punishment
state of innocence as evidence of pre-moral defectibility

HuYgTa-159627-d1e791.summary: Second argument: the power to fail through corruption is present in corruptible created things from God; therefore the power to fail through choice, which is the power to sin, is likewise present in things capable of choosing, from God himself. The antecedent is proved because whatever the order of the universe necessarily requires belongs to things from God, and having the power to fail through corruption is required by the order of the universe (e.g., plants could not be nourished if earth could not decay, nor beasts nourished by plants, nor humans by beasts, without such corruptibility).
claims: By analogy with the God-given power of corruptible things to fail (required for the universe's nutritive order), the power to sin (a power to fail through choice) should likewise be traced to God.
concepts: order of the universe requiring corruptibility
analogy between corruption and moral failure

HuYgTa-159627-d1e813.summary: Third argument: that a creature is from nothing is from God himself; but the power to sin belongs to a creature precisely because it is from nothing, according to the rival opinion itself; therefore the power to sin belongs to the creature from God. The major is proved by the principle that whatever is the cause of an affirmation is also the cause of the negation that per se and immediately follows from it (just as what causes health also causes the corresponding absence of sickness); but God is the cause of the creature according to every positive entity in it, so God is the cause of the creature's being from nothing and from no presupposed matter, since this negative follows per se and necessarily from that positive fact.
claims: Using the rival opinion's own premise (that defectibility follows from being made ex nihilo, which is itself from God), the author argues that God, as cause of the creature's positive being ex nihilo, is thereby also cause of the associated negative fact and its consequences, including the power to sin.
concepts: cause of affirmation as cause of consequent negation
creation ex nihilo as caused by God

HuYgTa-159627-d1e846.summary: Draws together the replies to the original four objections. Reply to the first (implicitly, via the preceding arguments): being from nothing does not belong to the creature of itself but from God; when it is said that a creature left to itself tends toward nothing, the sufficient cause of that tendency is God himself — not through his positive influence and operation, but through the subtraction of his influence, since whatever is, through its influence, the total and perfect cause of some entity and its conservation will, through the subtraction of that influence, be the sufficient cause of that entity's falling into nothing; and God, through his influence, is the perfect cause of every created entity and of the conservation of the whole creature, which is conserved in some being.
claims: God is the sufficient cause of a creature's tendency toward nothingness, not by positive operation but by the subtraction of his sustaining influence, since he is the total and perfect cause of the creature's positive being and conservation.
concepts: causality by subtraction of influence (negative causality)
God as total cause of created being and conservation

HuYgTa-159627-d1e877.summary: Reply to the second original objection (from Anselm, that sinning is not liberty or part of liberty): denies the minor. To its proof: although sinning is not itself liberty, the ability to sin (posse peccare) is within the liberty of our free will; nonetheless our will would be freer if it could not sin, since the liberty of the blessed, who cannot sin, is greater than that of wayfarers, who can.
claims: Though sinning is not liberty, the ability to sin belongs to free will's liberty; yet a will incapable of sin (as in the blessed) possesses greater liberty than one capable of sin (as in wayfarers).
concepts: liberty of the blessed vs. liberty of wayfarers

HuYgTa-159627-d1e896.summary: Reply to the third original objection (act more perfect than potency, so sin would be from God): denies the consequence. To its proof: although in good things act is nobler than potency, in bad things the reverse holds, since it is worse actually to be sick than merely to be able to be sick.
claims: The 'act is nobler than potency' principle is reversed for evils: actual sickness (or sin) is worse than mere potency for it, blocking the inference that sin's actuality must be more clearly traced to God than its mere potency.
concepts: asymmetry of act/potency nobility between goods and evils

HuYgTa-159627-d1e909.summary: Notes an alternative addition found elsewhere: one can also say that although sin itself is not from God, the act of sinning is from God in the sense already explained (i.e., as a positive act-entity, though not under its sinful deformity).
claims: An alternative gloss: the act of sinning (considered as positive entity) is from God, though sin as such (its moral deformity) is not.
concepts: distinguishing the positive act from its sinful deformity

HuYgTa-159627-d1e920.summary: Reply to the fourth original objection (evil use implies evil nature): concedes that what is evil in such a way that its use is necessarily evil (such that we cannot use it well) is itself evil, but denies this of something whose use is evil only because, though we could use it well, we instead abuse it — such a thing is not evil but can be good, since we can also misuse good things (which is more properly called abuse than use); but the power to sin, which is free will, we can, if we wish, use well by resisting vice and pursuing virtue.
claims: The power to sin (free will) is not evil, because its evil use is a contingent abuse rather than a necessary use — free will can instead be used well, resisting vice and pursuing virtue.
concepts: necessary evil use vs. contingent abuse
free will's capacity for good use

HuYgTa-159627-d1e949.summary: Heading paragraph for Article 4, restating its question: whether every power to dominate is from God.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e958.summary: Announces two matters to be examined under Article 4: first, whether every prelacy/power to dominate is from God; second, whether a faithful (Christian) person is bound to obey an infidel lord or prince.
claims: Article 4 divides into whether dominion as such is from God, and whether Christians must obey an infidel ruler.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e970.summary: States that dominion/rulership (principatus) can be considered three ways: in itself, according to the mode by which one obtains it, and according to its use.
claims: Principatus admits a threefold consideration: in itself, in its mode of acquisition, and in its use.
concepts: threefold consideration of dominion (in se, modus consequendi, usus)

HuYgTa-159627-d1e980.summary: States the first conclusion: taking dominion in the first way (in itself), all dominion is from God.
claims: Dominion considered in itself is from God.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e990.summary: First proof (argument 1): every good is from God; but dominion considered in itself, being a certain order or mode of ordered vision (of the universe), is no small good of the universe; therefore it is from God.
claims: Dominion, considered as an ordering principle contributing to the good of the universe, is from God as every good is.
concepts: dominion as ordering good of the universe

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1003.summary: Second proof (argument 2): the first is always the cause of all other subsequent things; but God is the first prince of the whole universe (per Metaphysics II and XII); therefore all dominion is from God.
claims: As first cause and first prince of the universe (per Aristotle's Metaphysics), God is the cause of all subsequent dominion.
concepts: God as first prince of the universe

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1015.summary: Third proof (argument 3): whatever would have existed in paradise had man remained in the state of innocence is from God; but dominion in the described sense would have existed in paradise, since naturally those excelling in prudence and intellect rule (as in Politics I: man over child, male over female, human over beasts), and even in paradise one human would have been more apt than another in intellectual habits and acts, owing to superior bodily complexion (citing the Aristotelian tag that 'soft-fleshed are apt in mind, hard-fleshed inept,' properly understood of complexion's goodness/rarity, not of an excess of phlegm as in women); and such differences in complexion, arising from the conjunction of the stars at conception, would have existed then as now.
claims: Dominion in the sense of natural intellectual precedence would have existed even in the state of innocence, since bodily-complexional differences producing differences in intellectual aptitude would have obtained in paradise as they do now.
Natural rule follows from superior prudence/intellect (Politics I): man over child, male over female, human over beast.
concepts: De anima II citation on complexion

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1057.summary: First objection against dominion existing in paradise: no dominion can exist without servitude, but there would have been no servitude in paradise; the major is proved because one of a pair of relatives cannot exist without the other (per the Categories and Metaphysics V); the minor is proved because servitude was introduced only on account of sin.
claims: Since dominion and servitude are correlative and servitude only entered through sin, there could have been no dominion in the sinless state of paradise.
concepts: Aristotle's Categories and Metaphysics V on relatives

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1075.summary: Second objection: every dominion employs some law with respect to its subjects; but 'the law is not laid down for the just,' per the Apostle (1 Timothy 1:9); since in the state of innocence all would have been perfectly just by original justice, there would have been no law, and hence no dominion, in paradise; confirmed by Ethics X, that laws with coercive power were instituted only on account of the rebellious and unjust, whereas in the state of innocence no one would have been rebellious or unjust.
claims: Since dominion requires law, and law (per 1 Timothy) is not for the just, and all would have been perfectly just in paradise, there would have been no law and hence no dominion there.
concepts: law not laid down for the just (1 Timothy 1:9)
coercive law and its purpose (Ethics X)

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1099.summary: Responds by distinguishing dominion two ways: (1) as concerning a servile fear that excludes affection in the subject — this is despotic dominion, requiring a punitive servitude introduced on account of sin, and would not have obtained between humans in the state of innocence, only between humans and irrational animals (per God's command to Adam and Eve to have dominion over fish, birds, and animals, and later to Noah's sons over the beasts' terror and dread); (2) as concerning mutual affection, which is twofold — according to free will (regal dominion, which would have obtained between parents and children in paradise) or according to fixed laws (political dominion, which would have obtained between husband and wife, the more prudent ruling the less prudent politically according to laws promoting the good of matrimony, for their benefit).
claims: Despotic dominion (servile, punitive) presupposes sin and would only have applied to human dominion over animals in paradise, not between humans.
Regal dominion (parents over children, by free affection) and political dominion (husband over wife, by fixed beneficial laws) would have existed in paradise without implying servitude or injustice.
concepts: distinguishing dominion by mode of subjection

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1159.summary: Notes this distinction resolves the first objection, and turns to the second: replies that among us there are three effects of prelacy — teaching subjects how to be better directed in their acts, defending subjects from unjust oppression, and punishing bad subjects to correct their excesses; in paradise, the first mode of law and prelacy would have existed, but not the second and third — and the authorities cited from the Apostle and the Philosopher concern these latter two modes.
claims: Prelacy has three effects (teaching, defending, punishing); only the teaching function would have obtained in paradise, so the cited authorities against law/dominion in paradise apply only to the punitive/defensive functions, not the teaching one.
concepts: threefold effect of prelacy (docere, defendere, punire)
restricting the scope of the cited authorities

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1183.summary: Additional positive argument for the conclusion that dominion is from God: whatever befits human beings according to right reason befits them from God, i.e., according to divine ordination; but according to right reason there ought to be prelacy/dominion among humans; therefore dominion is from God. The major is proved because God gives reason to man in order to carry out what right reason requires; the minor is proved because whatever is natural and expedient is according to right reason, and (per Politics I) in every ordered plurality it is natural and expedient that one preside and others be subject, which is precisely what constitutes the notion of prelacy.
claims: Dominion is from God because it befits human beings according to right reason, which itself is God's gift ordered toward what right reason requires; and ordered rule (one presiding, others subject) is natural and expedient in any ordered plurality, per Aristotle's Politics I.
concepts: right reason as measure of what is from God
natural hierarchy in ordered pluralities (Politics I)

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1214.summary: Confirms the preceding argument by analogy with the natural order generally: in all natural things we observe that inferior things are ruled by superior things, and multitude is reduced to unity; and custom, like art, ought to imitate nature.
claims: The rule of superior over inferior and reduction of multitude to unity, observable throughout nature, confirms by analogy that hierarchical dominion among humans (custom imitating nature) is likewise natural and God-given.
concepts: hierarchy in nature as analogy for human dominion

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1227.summary: Turns to the second and third considerations (mode of acquiring dominion, and its use): if dominion is acquired and used in an orderly way, observing the due requirements of law (proper conditions and circumstances in its acquisition and use), then such prelacy or rule is from God; but if these are not observed, then although such prelacy and rule remain from God as to the nature and entitative reality of the acts (just as other evil acts are from God, as proved above), they are not from God as to the deformity and obliquity of the act, since mortal sin is committed in such cases, which cannot be from God but from an evil human will — hence such rulers are addressed in Hosea 8:4, 'they reigned, but not by me; they set up princes, and I knew it not,' i.e., with the knowledge of approval.
claims: Dominion acquired and used in accordance with due legal order is fully from God.
Dominion acquired or used disorderly remains from God as to the entitative reality of the acts, but its moral deformity (mortal sin) is from the evil human will, not from God, per Hosea 8:4.
concepts: distinguishing entitative reality of an act from its moral deformity

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1264.summary: Applies the preceding distinction to resolve common objections (that some principalities are perverse, others usurped, others justly taken away): just as 'what God has joined, man must not separate,' so what someone has been given by God cannot rightly be taken away by man; these objections concern only the disordered mode of acquiring or the disordered use of dominion — for one can justly acquire dominion yet use it so perversely as to deserve deprivation of it by right.
claims: Common objections about perverse, usurped, or forfeited principalities are resolved by noting they concern only disordered acquisition or use of dominion, not dominion's divine origin as such; even justly acquired dominion can be justly forfeited through perverse use.
concepts: Matthew 19:6 ('what God has joined...') applied analogically to dominion

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1297.summary: Turns to the second part of Article 4 (whether Christians must obey an infidel prince), setting up a threefold division: such an infidel is either (1) justly consecuted his dominion and uses it in an orderly way, or (2) unjustly consecuted his dominion, or (3) justly acquired dominion but uses it unjustly and disorderly.
claims: The question of obedience to an infidel prince is analyzed by a threefold division of cases concerning the justice of his acquisition and use of dominion.
concepts: threefold case division for obedience to an infidel ruler

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1314.summary: States the response to the first case: such Christian subjects are bound to obey such a prince, even though he is an infidel, unless they have been justly freed from such servitude by some means, such as through a superior prince who has full dominion over that infidel lord; but in the second and third cases (described in the following paragraphs), they say the subjects are not bound to obey such an infidel lord.
claims: Christians must obey a justly-ruling infidel prince (case 1), unless freed by a superior authority; but are not bound to obey in cases of unjust acquisition or unjust use (cases 2 and 3).
concepts: obedience to a justly-ruling infidel prince

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1338.summary: First proof for case 1: what someone has justly acquired cannot be unjustly taken from him unless he abuses it; but this infidel, as supposed, has justly acquired such dominion and has not abused it; therefore (his subjects owe him obedience, and his dominion should not be removed).
claims: Since the infidel prince in case 1 has justly acquired and not abused his dominion, it cannot justly be taken from him, supporting continued obedience.
concepts: justly acquired possessions cannot be unjustly removed absent abuse

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1351.summary: Second proof, citing 1 Peter 2:18 (Blessed Peter speaking of Christians): 'Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wayward.'
claims: 1 Peter 2:18 is cited as scriptural support for Christian obedience even to harsh (though not unjust) masters.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1362.summary: Third proof, citing the Apostle (1 Timothy 6:1): 'Whoever are under the yoke of servitude should regard their masters as worthy of all honor,' with the Gloss explaining 'yoke' as the yoke of infidel masters.
claims: 1 Timothy 6:1, with its Gloss specifying 'infidel masters,' further supports the obligation of servants (Christians) to honor even infidel lords.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1382.summary: Fourth proof, citing Romans 13:1: 'Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.'
claims: Romans 13:1 is cited as general scriptural support for subjection to ruling powers, including infidel ones.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1391.summary: Fifth proof: divine law, which comes from grace and Christian faith, does not abolish what belongs to human law and natural reason; but the distinction between the faithful and infidel is from divine law, whereas just dominion is from human law and natural reason; therefore (the distinction of faithful/infidel does not abolish just dominion). The major is proved by the analogy that grace does not abolish human nature but perfects it, so divine law does not abolish what is of human law and springs from right reason; hence the distinction of faithful from infidel does not abolish the dominion of an infidel lord over a faithful subject.
claims: Since divine law (like grace) perfects rather than abolishes natural/human law, and just dominion belongs to natural/human law, the faith-based distinction between believer and infidel does not by itself abolish an infidel's just dominion over a faithful subject.
concepts: grace perfects nature (analogy applied to law)
distinguishing divine law from natural/human law

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1399.summary: Reports a rival opinion held by certain doctors: the dominion that an infidel prince holds over a Christian people can, by the church's own authority, be justly taken away from such a prince.
claims: A rival view holds that the church can, by its own authority, justly strip an infidel prince of dominion over a Christian people.
concepts: ecclesiastical authority to depose infidel rulers

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1429.summary: First argument for this rival opinion: an infidel deserves, by the demerit of his infidelity, to lose the power he had over those who have been translated into sons of God.
claims: An infidel's own infidelity is a demerit sufficient to forfeit his power over those who have become children of God through faith.
concepts: demerit of infidelity as ground for forfeiture of power

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1440.summary: Second argument, citing the Savior's words (John 8:36): 'If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed'; but the Son of God has redeemed and freed by his blood every baptized person.
claims: John 8:36, applied to the redemptive freedom won by Christ's blood for the baptized, supports the rival view that Christian baptism entails freedom from infidel dominion.
concepts: redemption by Christ's blood as grounding liberty

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1451.summary: Third argument: the Savior says that sons are free from tribute; but power was given to all those regenerated in Christ, 'who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God,' to become sons of God, per John 1:12-13.
claims: Citing John 1:12-13 on the sonship of the regenerate, the rival view infers that baptized Christians, as sons, are free from the 'tribute' of servitude to infidel lords.
concepts: sonship of God and freedom from tribute

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1469.summary: Fourth argument: when the cause ceases, the effect ceases; but sin, which is the cause of servitude, ceases through baptism; therefore (servitude to an infidel lord should cease at baptism).
claims: Since baptism removes sin (the cause of servitude, per this argument), the effect — servitude to an infidel lord — should likewise cease.
concepts: sin as the cause of servitude

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1480.summary: Fifth argument: what absolves from a greater bond can also absolve from a lesser one; but faith absolves from the bond of marriage by which a believer was bound, before receiving the faith, to an infidel spouse (a bond seemingly greater and more intimate than servitude, since instituted by God in paradise, and confirmed by the Savior's words in the Gospel, 'what God has joined, man must not separate'); therefore faith should all the more be able to absolve a believer from the bond of an infidel lord.
claims: An a fortiori argument: since faith can dissolve the greater bond of marriage to an infidel spouse (a divinely instituted bond), it should also dissolve the lesser bond of servitude to an infidel lord.
concepts: Pauline privilege analogy (marriage to an infidel spouse)
a fortiori argument from greater to lesser bond

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1504.summary: States the author's own view, with reservation ('saving always the better judgment'): he does not hold the rival opinion. First counterargument: one who is not under the church's jurisdiction, except insofar as he sins against the church only in not holding the church's faith, cannot be justly punished by the church; but this infidel is supposed to have sinned against the church in no other respect than in not holding the church's faith; and the lord is gravely punished precisely by having the jurisdiction of his dominion, which he holds over his own servants, taken from him; therefore (he cannot be justly deprived of it by the church).
claims: The author rejects the rival view, arguing the church lacks jurisdiction to punish (by deposition) an infidel whose only 'offense' is not holding the church's faith, since that offense alone does not place him under the church's punitive jurisdiction.
concepts: limits of ecclesiastical jurisdiction over non-Christians
mere unbelief as insufficient ground for punishment

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1529.summary: Second counterargument: no infidel who has never been subject to the church's faith should be violently compelled to accept the church's faith; but if the church freed everyone newly coming to the faith from servitude owed to an infidel lord, such a lord would be violently compelled toward the faith, since any of his servants could convert to the faith and he would thereby lose his entire dominion unless he himself accepted the Christian faith.
claims: Granting the rival view's proposed liberation-upon-conversion policy would effectively coerce infidel lords into conversion (to avoid losing all their servants/dominion), violating the principle against forced conversion.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1551.summary: Raises a possible objection drawing on canon law ('extra de Iudaeis'): it is stated that if a servant of Jews becomes Christian, he is immediately freed from servitude, whether he was born into servitude ('vernaculus') or purchased into it ('emptitius').
claims: A canon-law provision (Extra, De Iudaeis) is cited as granting immediate freedom to a Jewish-owned servant upon conversion to Christianity, whether born or purchased into servitude.
concepts: canon law on servants of Jews converting to Christianity

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1571.summary: A further objection: if such a Christian remained under the yoke of this infidel prince, then that infidel lord could compel the subject to abandon the Christian faith and blaspheme Christ.
claims: Leaving a converted subject under an infidel lord's power risks the lord compelling him to apostatize and blaspheme, which is presented as an objection to the author's position.
concepts: risk of compelled apostasy under continued infidel rule

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1584.summary: Responds that the case of Jews and other infidels differs: the Jews, on account of their own demerit, were reduced to servitude and made proper slaves by the Roman princes (a servant being so called from 'being preserved,' since one taken justly by right of war and liable to be killed is instead spared and thereby reduced, with his posterity, to servitude — as happened to the Jews under Titus and Vespasian); since the Roman princes in due course became Christian, the Roman church can, in favor of the faith, free the servants of the Jews who convert to the faith, because the Jews and their goods are subject to the church's authority through the favor of the Roman emperors who conferred this upon the church — but this does not hold for other infidels.
claims: The canon-law liberation of converted Jewish servants is explained by the Jews' specific historical subjection (via conquest under Titus/Vespasian) to Roman authority, later transferred to the Christianized Roman church — a special case not extending to other infidels.
concepts: historical subjection of the Jews to Rome (Titus, Vespasian)
transfer of authority over the Jews to the Roman church

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1617.summary: Responds to the second instance/objection (risk of compelled apostasy): if an infidel prince compelled a faithful subject to deny the faith, he would thereby abuse his power, and for this would deserve to lose it, and a just war could even be waged against him and his dominion by the church and all Christians, to the point that not only could the subjects be justly freed from his dominion, but his own person could justly be reduced to servitude or even deprived of everything.
claims: The risk of compelled apostasy is addressed not by denying legitimate infidel dominion generally, but by holding that actually compelling apostasy constitutes an abuse of power justifying forfeiture, just war, liberation of subjects, and even enslavement or deprivation of the offending prince.
concepts: abuse of power through compelled apostasy as grounds for just war and forfeiture

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1641.summary: Reply to the first motive of the rival opinion (that an infidel deserves to lose power by demerit of infidelity alone): unless the infidel prince abuses his power in some other way, mere infidelity does not merit its loss.
claims: Mere infidelity, absent abuse of power, is not sufficient grounds to lose one's dominion — directly rejecting the rival opinion's first argument.
concepts: insufficiency of mere infidelity as grounds for forfeiture

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1653.summary: Reply to the second motive (John 8:36 on the Son's liberation): those words of Christ can be understood of the liberty by which Christians were freed from the servitude of the Mosaic law, i.e., from the observance of ceremonial precepts; they can also be understood of the liberty by which we are freed from sin and the devil's servitude.
claims: John 8:36 is reinterpreted as referring to liberation from Mosaic ceremonial law or from sin/the devil, not to liberation from civil servitude to an infidel lord.
concepts: reinterpreting John 8:36 away from civil liberty

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1669.summary: Reply to the third motive (sons free from tribute, John 1): Christ there means by 'sons' the Apostles, who, as Peter testifies ('behold, we have left all things and followed you'), possessed nothing of this world's goods, and so were not bound to pay tribute; but to the Jews, who did possess worldly goods, Christ said, 'render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's' — meaning, you owe tribute concerning the temporal goods you possess.
claims: The 'sons free from tribute' saying is restricted to the propertyless Apostles, not extended to all the baptized generally; property-owners (like the Jews addressed) still owe temporal tribute, per 'render unto Caesar.'
concepts: restricting 'sons free from tribute' to the Apostles

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1691.summary: Reply to the fourth motive (cessation of the cause of servitude at baptism): although through grace, charity, and the catholic faith received in baptism the soul is freed from the evil of fault, the body is not thereby freed from the evil of punishment — the baptized dies just as the unbaptized does, nor are we freed by faith from the debt of justice; rather, it is just to obey one's prince, even if an infidel, provided he has justly acquired his dominion and uses it justly and in an orderly way.
claims: Baptism frees the soul from the guilt of sin but not the body from temporal punishment/obligation, so the debt of civil obedience to a just (even infidel) ruler survives baptism.
concepts: distinguishing freedom from guilt vs. freedom from temporal penalty/obligation

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1713.summary: Reply to the fifth motive (the marriage-bond analogy): if one spouse converts to the faith while the other remains an infidel, and the infidel spouse consents to cohabit with the believer without disturbing them or enticing them to infidelity, and without blaspheming the Creator, then the believer is not released from the marriage bond; but if the infidel spouse refuses to cohabit except by enticing the believer to infidelity or blaspheming the Creator, then by his own demerit he forfeits his right over the believing spouse, who is consequently justly released — this is treated more fully in Book 4. Applies the same logic to political servitude: if an infidel prince demands from a faithful subject nothing beyond what he may justly demand, the subject must obey; but if he tries to force the subject into matters contrary to God and the soul's salvation, the infidel prince forfeits the right he had over that subject.
claims: The marriage-bond case (Pauline privilege logic) is resolved conditionally on whether the infidel party threatens the believer's faith; the same conditional logic (obedience unless faith/salvation is threatened) is extended to political servitude under an infidel prince.
concepts: conditional forfeiture of an infidel ruler's authority when faith is threatened

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1757.summary: States the second main conclusion (case 2 of the earlier threefold division): if a prince has unjustly acquired his dominion, then subjects are not bound to obey him, and may justly withdraw from him.
claims: Subjects of a prince who has unjustly acquired his dominion are not bound to obedience and may justly withdraw.

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1768.summary: Proof: from an unjust possessor, what he possesses unjustly can justly be taken away; but such a tyrant, as supposed, unjustly possesses this dominion; therefore (his subjects are not bound to obey, and it may justly be taken from him).
claims: An unjust possessor of dominion (a tyrant) can justly be deprived of it, since unjust possession does not generate a valid claim.
concepts: unjust possession does not generate valid claim

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1780.summary: States the third main conclusion (case 3): granted that an infidel prince has justly acquired his dominion, if he nevertheless uses it unjustly — for instance, by blaspheming the Creator or impeding a subject in matters pertaining to the Christian faith — he again deserves to lose such dominion.
claims: Even justly acquired dominion is forfeited if used unjustly, especially by blasphemy or impeding a subject's Christian faith.
concepts: forfeiture through unjust use despite just acquisition

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1796.summary: Offers a persuasive argument for the third conclusion, though it already follows from what precedes: whenever the same subject is obligated to two lords, one as simply superior and the other as inferior, if the inferior prince compels that subject to dissent from fidelity to the superior lord, the inferior prince, according to laws and rights, forfeits jurisdiction over that subject, who is no longer bound to obey him; but God is the supreme lord and universal emperor, in relation to whom every prince of this world is inferior; therefore (an infidel prince who compels a subject away from fidelity to God forfeits jurisdiction over that subject).
claims: By the general legal principle that an inferior lord forfeits jurisdiction by compelling disloyalty to a superior lord, and since God is the supreme lord over all earthly princes, an infidel prince who compels disloyalty to God forfeits his jurisdiction.
concepts: hierarchy of superior and inferior lords
God as supreme lord and universal emperor

HuYgTa-159627-d1e1825.summary: Closing reply to the principal argument of the whole question (the 1 John 'sin unto death' text): Blessed John did not intend that any sin, however great, is totally irremissible while a person lives in this world, but rather that it is very difficult to obtain remission of such most wicked sins, so that they are not brought to due penitence through the prayer of just any mediocre Christian, but only through the prayer of excellent and most devout believers. Alternatively, John by 'sin unto death' might mean sin against the Holy Spirit under the circumstance of final impenitence: where it is certainly known that someone departed this life in mortal sin without penitence, one should not pray for that person according to the common rule of the Church, since such a person is outside the state of meriting — in which state may the Savior of all who are to be saved, who lives and reigns forever and ever, Amen, preserve us for the way of our present pilgrimage until he leads us to the homeland of blessed enjoyment.
claims: 1 John's 'sin unto death' does not mean a sin absolutely irremissible in this life, but one whose remission is exceptionally difficult, obtainable only through the prayer of especially devout believers.

Alternatively, the 'sin unto death' may refer specifically to sin against the Holy Spirit under the circumstance of final impenitence, for which the Church's common rule withholds prayer once death without penitence is certain.
concepts: the Church's rule on praying for the certainly impenitent dead

HuYgTa-159627-Dd1e188.summary: Article 1 (Utrum sit aliquod peccatum in spiritum sanctum): establishes that Scripture plainly attests a sin against the Holy Spirit, distinguishing it (taken essentially, as deity, not merely personally) from remissible blasphemy against Christ's humanity, per Matthew 12:32 and the ancient doctors' reading, versus a 'modern' reading in terms of appropriated divine attributes. Surveys and organizes competing enumerations of such sins (four, six, or eight) using a fourfold analytic scheme (physician/medicine/patient/sickness — God's justice and mercy misjudged as despair and presumption; faith and grace rendered useless as impugning truth and envying grace; the sinner's pertinacity as obstinacy and impenitence; the sin's own habitual/terminal character as malicious habit and final impenitence), concluding that properly speaking there are four distinct species of such sin (despair, presumption, impugning the truth of faith, envy of grace), with the remaining four items better classified as circumstances or consequences applicable to any mortal sin.
claims: There is a sin against the Holy Spirit, understood essentially (as deity) and distinguished from remissible blasphemy against Christ's humanity.

Properly speaking there are four species of sin against the Holy Spirit — despair, presumption, impugning the truth of faith, and envy of a neighbor's grace — with obstinacy, resolve never to repent, habitual malice, and final impenitence being circumstances rather than distinct species.

HuYgTa-159627-Dd1e464.summary: Article 2 (Utrum peccatum in spiritum sanctum sit irremissibile): concludes that, with respect to divine power, no sin whatsoever is irremissible — God could remit any sin — but sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible in a qualified sense, since unlike excusable sins it contains no attached excusing circumstance (only aggravating ones), giving it no 'aptitude' toward remission, and it renders the sinner impenitent, which further blocks remission absent penitence. Considers and rejects an Augustinian-inspired rival view holding such sin (as mortal sin joined with final impenitence) simply irremissible in an unqualified sense, objecting that infinite divine power cannot be exhausted by any sin, and citing the widely reported legend of Trajan's posthumous deliverance through Gregory's prayers as a counterexample to strict irremissibility even after death.
claims: No sin is irremissible relative to divine power itself.
Sin against the Holy Spirit is 'irremissible' only in the qualified sense of lacking any excusing circumstance and inducing impenitence, not in the sense of being beyond God's power to remit.
The Trajan legend and the inexhaustibility of divine power tell against the rival view that such sin is simply and unqualifiedly irremissible.
concepts: irremissibility as lack of aptitude vs. lack of divine power

HuYgTa-159627-Dd1e606.summary: Article 3 (Utrum omnis potentia peccandi sit a Deo): concludes that the power to sin is from God, proved because it is a genuine (positive) being traceable to God as first cause (John 1:3), because it is identical with the power to do good and merit (rational powers extending to opposites), because it resides in the will (itself from God, per Augustine), and because powers for evil are themselves classified as good (per Aristotle's Topics). Engages a rival distinction (power to sin as act-principle is from God, but its defectibility is not, being a consequence of creation ex nihilo) and Anselm-based and act/potency-based objections, accepting the first half of the distinction but rejecting the denial that defectibility is from God — arguing instead that God, as total and perfect cause of a creature's positive being and conservation, is also the sufficient (negative) cause of its capacity to fail when his sustaining influence is withdrawn. Concludes by resolving the four original objections: the ability to sin belongs to free will's liberty even though a will incapable of sin (as in the blessed) is freer; act being nobler than potency is reversed for evils; and the power to sin's evil use is a contingent abuse, not a necessary evil, since free will can also be used well.
claims: The power to sin is from God, both as a positive act-principle and, against a rival view, in its defectibility, since God is the sufficient cause (by withdrawal of sustaining influence) of a creature's capacity to fail.
The power to sin is not itself evil, since its evil use (unlike a necessarily evil thing's use) is a contingent abuse of a capacity that can also be used well.

HuYgTa-159627-Dd1e961.summary: Article 4 (Utrum omnis potentia dominandi sit a Deo): divides into whether dominion as such is from God and whether Christians must obey an infidel ruler. On the first question, concludes that dominion considered in itself is from God (as a good ordering the universe, traceable to God as first cause per Aristotle, and would have existed even in the state of innocence in the form of natural precedence by intellectual/prudential excellence — parents over children, husband over wife — though not despotic dominion, which presupposes sin and servitude); dominion considered as to its mode of acquisition and use is from God only when exercised in accordance with due legal order, otherwise remaining from God only as to the entitative reality of the act, not its moral deformity (per Hosea 8:4). On the second question, distinguishes three cases of infidel rulership — justly acquired and justly used (subjects must obey, per 1 Peter 2:18, 1 Timothy 6:1, Romans 13:1, and the principle that divine law does not abolish natural/human law, against a rival view that the church may depose such a ruler merely for infidelity), unjustly acquired (subjects need not obey and may justly withdraw), and justly acquired but unjustly used, e.g. by compelling apostasy (again forfeiting jurisdiction, since God as supreme lord takes precedence over any inferior prince) — and closes the whole question by reinterpreting 1 John's 'sin unto death' as denoting either the extreme difficulty (not strict impossibility) of obtaining remission for the gravest sins, or specifically sin against the Holy Spirit compounded by final impenitence, for which the Church withholds prayer once death without repentance is certain.
claims: Dominion in itself, and dominion exercised in due legal order, is from God; disorderly acquisition or use remains from God only as to the act's entitative reality, not its moral deformity.

Christians must obey a justly-ruling infidel prince, but need not obey one whose dominion is unjustly acquired or unjustly used (e.g., through compelling apostasy), since such misuse forfeits jurisdiction before God as supreme lord.
The Church lacks authority to depose an infidel ruler for infidelity alone, absent abuse of power.
The 'sin unto death' of 1 John is reinterpreted as denoting extreme difficulty of remission or specifically final-impenitent sin against the Holy Spirit, not strict irremissibility.
concepts: final reinterpretation of 1 John's 'sin unto death'

HuYgTa-159627.summary: Quaestio 1, 'An peccatum aliquod sit simpliciter irremissibile' (Whether any sin is simply irremissible), resolves the question across four articles corresponding to the material of distinctions 43-44: whether there is a sin against the Holy Spirit (Article 1, answered affirmatively and analyzed into four proper species via a physician/medicine/patient/sickness scheme); whether that sin is irremissible (Article 2, answered only in the qualified sense of lacking any excusing circumstance and inducing impenitence, never in the sense of exceeding God's power); whether every power to sin is from God (Article 3, answered affirmatively both as to the power's positive act-principle and, against a rival view, as to its defectibility, which God causes negatively by withdrawing his sustaining influence); and whether every power to dominate is from God (Article 4, answered affirmatively for dominion in itself and for its licit acquisition/use, with a further resolution of whether Christians must obey an infidel ruler — yes if his rule is just, no if unjustly acquired or abusively exercised). The overall resolutio states that no sin is irremissible relative to divine power, yet sin against the Holy Spirit is rightly called irremissible because it contains no excusing circumstance, even though its very capacity to be committed ultimately flowed from God.
claims: No sin is irremissible with respect to God's absolute power; sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible only because it lacks any excusing circumstance.
There are properly four species of sin against the Holy Spirit.
The power to sin, including its defectibility, is from God, though sin's moral deformity is from the evil human will.
Dominion as such, and its just exercise, is from God; obedience is owed to a justly-ruling infidel prince but not to one whose rule is unjustly acquired or abusively used.
